name: The Secretary Problem
statement: Look at the first 37 percent, then take the next one better than all of them.
statementAccent: the next one better than all
meaning: You interview candidates one at a time in random order, must accept or reject each on the spot with no going back, and want to choose the single best. The optimal strategy is to reject the first roughly thirty-seven per cent, using them only to set a benchmark, then accept the first later candidate who beats everyone seen so far. Remarkably, this both tells you how many to skip and gives your chance of landing the very best: about thirty-seven per cent, whatever the number of candidates.
mechanism: The rule embodies a look-then-leap tradeoff: an exploration phase that gathers information without committing, followed by an exploitation phase that seizes the first record-beating candidate. Skip too few and your benchmark is weak; skip too many and you have probably already passed the best. Working through the mathematics, the probability of success with a cutoff at a fraction of the candidates is that fraction times the negative logarithm of itself, which is maximised when the fraction is one over the mathematical constant e: about thirty-seven per cent, at which the success probability is also one over e.

examples.text: Martin Gardner popularised the puzzle in 1960 as the game of googol, choosing the largest of hidden numbers revealed one at a time: the framing that spread the problem widely.

Applied to dating, the rule says spend the first thirty-seven per cent of your candidates learning, then commit to the first partner who surpasses all of them: the exploration-exploitation model of the marriage problem.
Any sequential search under time pressure with no recall (hiring, apartment hunting, house buying) is a version of the same optimal-stopping problem.

variants.name: The cardinal-payoff version
variants.text: If you value the actual quality of your choice rather than only whether it is the single best, the optimal cutoff shifts from thirty-seven per cent toward the square root of the number of candidates.

variants.name: Robbins' problem
variants.text: The variant of minimising the expected rank of your choice rather than maximising the chance of the best, famously unsolved, with the optimal value known only to lie between about 1.9 and 2.3.

whyItMatters: It is the canonical model of optimal stopping and the exploration-exploitation dilemma, giving a clean, counterintuitive rule for deciding under sequential uncertainty with no second chances. Its thirty-seven per cent answer, appearing in dating, hiring, and search alike, is one of the most quoted results of applied probability, and a rare case where a hard decision has a precise mathematical guide.

working.text: spend the first thirty-seven per cent of your options learning without choosing, then take the first that beats them all.

working.lead: Match the goal to the rule
working.text: use the thirty-seven per cent cutoff only if you truly need the single best; if good enough will do, a different, earlier cutoff is better.
expect to succeed only about a third of the time even playing optimally, since the problem is genuinely hard.

limits: The classic result rests on strong assumptions: that you are credited only for the single best, with second-best counting as total failure; that rejected options are gone forever; that the number of candidates is known and fixed; that they arrive in random order; and that you have only their relative ranks. Real searches violate these. You can often recall an option, your chosen candidate may decline, the count may be unknown, and you usually value good rather than only best. Variants address each: the square-root cutoff for valuing quality, Bruss's rule for unknown counts, and the still-unsolved Robbins' problem for minimising expected rank. Experiments find people tend to stop too soon.
misreadings: The thirty-seven per cent rule does not maximise your chance of a good-enough match: it maximises the chance of getting the single best, and even then it succeeds only about a third of the time, failing two times in three. The fraction you skip and your probability of winning are both about thirty-seven per cent, but they are different quantities that happen to coincide. And the fraction does not grow with the number of candidates; it stays near thirty-seven per cent whether there are ten or ten million.
origin: Of murky origin, introduced by Merrill Flood around 1949 and popularised by Martin Gardner in Scientific American in 1960 as the game of googol; first solved in print by Dennis Lindley in 1961, with a Markov-chain treatment by Eugene Dynkin in 1963.
